title: Whoa! The Oldest Wooden Tools Ever Found Are 430,000 Years Old!
summary: Imagine holding a wooden stick that someone used 430,000 years ago. That’s older than any wooden tool ever found before! Scientists digging at a site called Marathousa 1 in Greece found two pieces of wood that early humans carefully shaped. One was from an alder tree, the other from willow or poplar. They had chop marks and signs of wear, like they were used for digging or stripping bark. That’s a huge deal because wood usually rots away. It needs special wet, muddy conditions to survive. This discovery pushes back the date for wooden tools by at least 40,000 years. The site also had stone tools and elephant bones, so people probably butchered animals there by an ancient lake. But not all the marks on the wood were from humans. One piece had deep grooves from a big carnivore—maybe a bear! That means early humans had to compete with scary predators for food. Professor Katerina Harvati, who leads the research, says this shows how clever and skilled these ancient people were. They weren’t just banging rocks together; they were shaping wood with real skill. So next time you pick up a stick, think about how long humans have been making tools just like that!
why_it_matters: This discovery shows that making and sharing tools is something humans have done for hundreds of thousands of years, which helps us appreciate the skills we learn from family and school today.

background_read: Before this find, the oldest known wooden tool was a spear tip found in England that is about 400,000 years old.
Wood usually rots away, so it survives only in wet, muddy ground like the ancient lake at Marathousa 1 in Greece.
Professor Katerina Harvati, a scientist who studies ancient humans, leads the team working at this site.
Article_Structure: WHO: early humans, Professor Katerina Harvati and her research team
WHAT: the discovery of two shaped wooden tools that are 430,000 years old, pushing back the age of wooden tools by at least 40,000 years
WHERE: Marathousa 1 site in Greece, near an ancient lake
WHY: because wet, muddy ground preserved the wood, and careful study shows how early humans shaped tools and competed with carnivores

perspectives.description: They see this as a huge leap in understanding how early humans thought and worked, proving they were more skilled than we once believed.
Some experts point out that natural forces like water or animals can make marks that look like human work, so they want more evidence before being completely sure.
They see this story as a powerful way to get kids excited about history and science, showing that everyday tools have a very, very long past.
